241.quote_or_event: “I have horses, elephants, and subjects, a town and a seraglio, power and command … how could he be without protection? Reverend sir, you speak untruth.” … “You are the protector of all unprotected beings, O ascetic.”
241.explanation: King Srenika boasts that his riches make him secure, but the young monk shows him that wealth protects no one, and the humbled king ends by calling the compassionate monk the protector of every unprotected being.
241.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the wealth of compassion above material wealth, which even the basest can hold; the Uttaradhyayana likewise sets a king's treasure below the monk's care for all beings.
241._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (ellipsis joins verses 14 and 15, then verse 56); the contrast of royal wealth with the protector of beings fits well, but the lecture is mainly about having no refuge, not a ranking of two kinds of wealth.

242.quote_or_event: “First the persuasion of every one should be ascertained, and then we will ask them severally: Ye professors! is pain pleasant to you, or unpleasant? If they give the right answer, reply: For all sorts of living beings pain is unpleasant, disagreeable. and greatly feared.”
242.explanation: The Acaranga answers rival teachers who claim to have examined the matter in every way and found killing harmless: tested properly, every inquiry leads back to the fact that all beings fear pain, so none should be harmed.
242.tie_back: Valluvar says that however many ways one examines the paths, compassion alone proves the true support; the Acaranga likewise says that honest inquiry from every side always arrives at non-harm.
242.source: Acaranga Sutra I.4.2.3-6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
242._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (the stray full stop after 'disagreeable' is in Jacobi's text); a strong fit for the kural's theme of examining many paths, though the Jain conclusion is framed as non-injury rather than as compassion being a 'companion'.

243.quote_or_event: “He who despises the Law that enjoins compassion, and praises the Law that permits slaughter, and who feeds but a single unprincipled man, even if he be a king, will go to darkness, and not to the gods.”
243.explanation: In his debate with a Vedic priest, the Jain monk Ardraka says that whoever rejects the law of compassion goes to darkness (Jacobi notes the original word literally means 'night').
243.tie_back: Valluvar says those whose hearts hold compassion never enter the dark world of suffering; Ardraka states the same truth from the other side, that those who scorn compassion go to darkness.
243._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the kural's compassion/darkness link but states the negative case, and it is set in a polemic against Vedic feeding of priests.

244.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
244.explanation: King Sanjaya, out hunting, kills a frightened deer, then trembles before the meditating monk Gardabhali, who tells him he need not fear but must give the same safety to every creature; the king renounces his throne.
244.tie_back: Valluvar says those who protect all living beings need never fear for themselves; Gardabhali links the king's own freedom from fear to his giving safety to all beings.
244._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the pairing of fearlessness with giving safety to others closely fits the kural, though the monk's assurance is personal, not a general law that the protector of life escapes the results of his own deeds.

245.quote_or_event: Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra lists compassion (anukampa) for all living beings and for those who keep vows, together with charity, self-restraint with some attachment, forbearance and purity, as the causes of the inflow of pleasant-feeling (sata-vedaniya) karma.
245.explanation: In Jain karma theory, compassion attracts the karma that later ripens as pleasant experience, while causing pain to others attracts karma that ripens as suffering.
245.tie_back: Valluvar says sorrow does not come to those who live by compassion; the Tattvartha Sutra gives the Jain mechanism, in which compassion binds karma whose fruit is pleasant feeling rather than pain.
245.source: Tattvartha Sutra 6.12 (Digambara numbering; 6.13 in the Svetambara recension), as given with commentary by Vijay K. Jain (wisdomlib.org)
245._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the sutra's content was confirmed through search summaries of the wisdomlib and jainworld renderings, but I did not check any translation's exact wording, so this is not quoted. A strong doctrinal fit, though it lacks the kural's appeal to the earth as witness.

246.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
246.explanation: The sage warns that a man without pity is ruined by his own perversity more surely than by any enemy, and will know it only at death.
246.tie_back: Valluvar says those who abandon compassion and do wrong have lost sight of life's real purpose; the Uttaradhyayana likewise says the pitiless man is ruined by his own perversity and learns too late what he has lost.
246._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial fit. It is addressed to a careless monk (Jacobi treats verses 38-53 as a later addition) and lacks the kural's point about forgetting one's own past suffering.

247.quote_or_event: “In vain he adopts nakedness, who errs about matters of paramount interest; neither this world nor the next will be his; he is a loser in both respects in the world.”
247.explanation: The sage says a false ascetic who goes wrong on what matters most loses both this world and the next.
247.tie_back: Valluvar matches this world, closed to the poor, with the other world, closed to the pitiless; the Uttaradhyayana uses the same this-world/next-world pairing for one who errs in what matters most, which in the passage includes being 'without pity' (20.48).
247._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; next-best match. It shares the two-worlds structure, but the verse concerns a lax monk rather than compassion as such, and has no wealth/compassion parallel.

248.quote_or_event: “The capital is human life, the gain is heaven; through the loss of that capital man must be born as a denizen of hell or a brute animal. … Having once forfeited them, he will have to endure these two states of misery; it will be difficult for him to attain an upward course for a long time to come.”
248.explanation: In the parable of three merchants, the one who loses his capital stands for the sinner who wastes human life, and the Sutra warns that such a loss is very hard to recover.
248.tie_back: Valluvar says those who lose wealth may flourish again, but those who lose compassion rarely recover; the Uttaradhyayana likewise sets ordinary loss against a moral loss from which the way back is long and hard.
248._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (ellipsis skips verse 17); the image of a loss that is hard to recover fits closely, but the lost 'capital' is a human birth wasted through sin, not compassion specifically.

249.quote_or_event: “Those who do not know this (Law), are not awakened, though they fancy themselves awakened; believing themselves awakened, they are beyond the boundary of right faith.”
249.explanation: Having just called non-killing 'the quintessence of wisdom', the Sutrakritanga says that those who miss this law only imagine they are enlightened and are in fact outside right faith.
249.tie_back: Valluvar likens virtue without compassion to a confused mind claiming to see the truth; the Sutrakritanga likewise says that those ignorant of the law of non-harm only fancy themselves awakened.
249._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the image of a deluded mind claiming insight fits closely, but the link to compassion depends on the verse's context (non-killing in I.11.9-10) rather than its own words.

250.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment.”
250.explanation: The Acaranga tells the would-be oppressor to put himself in his victim's place, and concludes that the righteous man therefore neither kills nor causes killing.
250.tie_back: Valluvar asks the strong to remember how they once trembled before someone stronger when they turn on the weak; the Acaranga gives the same exercise of imagined reversal at the moment one means to harm or tyrannise.
250.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
250._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near one-to-one fit in technique and timing, though the Acaranga asks one to imagine the victim's place rather than to recall one's own past fear.
